lessons.title: The Particle Model
lessons.description: States of matter, particle arrangements, and the limitations of the particle model.
lessons.content_html:
States of Matter

All matter exists in one of three states of matter: solid, liquid and gas. The particle model explains the differences between these states by describing how particles are arranged, how they move, and how strongly they are held together.

In a solid, particles are held in fixed positions by strong forces of attraction. They vibrate about these fixed positions but cannot move from place to place. This is why solids have a definite shape and a fixed volume. In a liquid, particles are close together but can move past each other. The forces of attraction are weaker than in a solid, giving liquids a fixed volume but no definite shape — they flow to fill the bottom of a container. In a gas, particles are far apart and move quickly in random directions. The forces of attraction are very weak, so gases have no fixed shape or volume and will spread out to fill any container.

Key Fact

Solids — particles in a regular arrangement, vibrate in fixed positions, close together. Liquids — particles close together but irregularly arranged, can slide past each other. Gases — particles far apart, move randomly at high speed.

Changes of State

When a substance is heated or cooled, it can change from one state to another. These are called changes of state. During a change of state, the particles themselves do not change — only the arrangement and movement of the particles change. This makes changes of state physical changes, not chemical changes, because they are reversible and no new substances are formed.

Melting — solid to liquid. Particles gain energy and overcome some of the forces holding them in fixed positions, so they can slide past each other. Boiling (or evaporation) — liquid to gas. Particles gain enough energy to overcome the remaining forces of attraction and escape into the air. Condensing — gas to liquid. Particles lose energy, slow down, and forces of attraction pull them closer together. Freezing — liquid to solid. Particles lose energy and lock into fixed positions. Sublimation — solid directly to gas without becoming a liquid first. Deposition — gas directly to solid.

During melting and boiling, energy is absorbed from the surroundings to break the forces between particles. During condensing and freezing, energy is released to the surroundings as new forces form between particles. Importantly, the temperature stays constant during a change of state — all the energy goes into breaking or forming intermolecular forces, not raising the temperature.

Key Fact

During a change of state, the temperature remains constant because the energy supplied is used to break (or form) forces between particles rather than increasing kinetic energy.

Heating and Cooling Curves

A heating curve is a graph of temperature against time for a substance being heated steadily. It shows: a rising section as the solid heats up, a flat section at the melting point (solid turning to liquid), a rising section as the liquid heats up, and a flat section at the boiling point (liquid turning to gas). The flat sections show that the substance is changing state — energy is being used to break intermolecular forces rather than raising the temperature.

A cooling curve shows the reverse process. The flat sections now represent condensation and freezing. A pure substance has sharp, flat plateaux at precise temperatures, while an impure substance changes state over a range of temperatures.

Physical Changes vs Chemical Changes

A physical change (such as a change of state) does not produce any new substances. The particles themselves stay the same — only their arrangement, spacing and energy change. Physical changes are reversible: ice can melt to water and then freeze back to ice. A chemical change forms new substances with different properties. Atoms are rearranged into new combinations. Chemical changes are usually irreversible under normal conditions — for example, burning magnesium in air produces magnesium oxide, which cannot easily be turned back into magnesium and oxygen.

The simple particle model represents particles as inelastic solid spheres (like bowling balls). This is useful for explaining states of matter and changes of state, but it has important limitations. The model does not account for the forces of attraction between particles, which are what actually hold substances together. It does not show that different particles have different sizes and masses. It does not represent the space between particles accurately — for example, gas particles are much further apart than diagrams usually show. It also fails to explain why different materials have different melting and boiling points, because it treats all particles as identical spheres. To explain differences in properties, we need to consider that the particles themselves (atoms, ions, molecules) and the bonds or forces between them are different in different substances.

Key Fact

The simple particle model (inelastic spheres) does not account for: forces of attraction between particles, different particle sizes, or the actual spacing between particles. It cannot explain why different materials have different properties.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When asked to “explain” changes of state, always refer to energy transfer and forces between particles — not forces within particles. A common mistake is saying particles “expand” or “get bigger” when heated. The particles themselves stay the same size; they gain kinetic energy and move further apart. For “compare” questions about physical and chemical changes, make a direct comparison in each sentence rather than describing each type separately.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The three states of matter differ in particle arrangement, movement and spacing. Solids have particles in fixed positions; liquids flow; gases spread out to fill their container.
  • Changes of state are physical changes — they are reversible and no new substances are formed. Temperature stays constant during a change of state.
  • The simple particle model has limitations: it does not account for forces between particles, different particle sizes, or why different materials have different properties.

lessons.title: Atomic Structure
lessons.description: Atomic models from Dalton to Bohr, sub-atomic particles, isotopes and ions.
lessons.content_html:
The Structure of the Atom

An atom is the smallest part of an element that can exist. Atoms are incredibly small — a typical atomic radius is about \(1 \times 10^{-10}\) m. Each atom has a tiny, dense nucleus at its centre. The nucleus contains two types of subatomic particle: protons (positive charge) and neutrons (no charge). Electrons orbit the nucleus in energy levels (shells) and carry a negative charge.

Key Fact

Relative charges and approximate relative masses: Proton — charge +1, mass 1. Neutron — charge 0, mass 1. Electron — charge −1, mass approximately \(\frac{1}{1836}\) (negligible). The nuclear radius is much smaller than the radius of the atom — most of the atom is empty space.

Atomic Number and Mass Number

The atomic number tells you the number of protons in the nucleus. It defines what element an atom is — all atoms of the same element have the same atomic number. In a neutral atom, the number of protons equals the number of electrons, so the atom has no overall charge. The mass number is the total number of protons plus neutrons.

To calculate the number of neutrons:

$$\text{number of neutrons} = \text{mass number} - \text{atomic number}$$

For example, sodium (Na) has atomic number 11 and mass number 23, so it has \(23 - 11 = 12\) neutrons, 11 protons and 11 electrons.

Isotopes and Ions

Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. This means they have different mass numbers but identical chemical properties. For example, carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons, while carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons.

An ion is an atom that has gained or lost electrons. Losing electrons forms a positive ion (cation) because there are now more protons than electrons. Gaining electrons forms a negative ion (anion). The nucleus does not change when an ion forms — only the number of electrons changes.

Standard notation shows mass number (top left), atomic number (bottom left) and chemical symbol. For example, \(^{23}_{11}\text{Na}\) tells you sodium has mass number 23 and atomic number 11. For ions, the charge is shown as a superscript: \(\text{Na}^+\) has lost one electron, \(\text{Cl}^-\) has gained one electron.

The Development of the Atomic Model

Our understanding of the atom has changed over time as new experimental evidence emerged.

Early 1800s

Dalton’s Model

John Dalton proposed atoms were tiny, solid, indivisible spheres. He thought all atoms of the same element were identical.

1897

Thomson’s Plum Pudding Model

J.J. Thomson discovered the electron and proposed a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.

1909–1911

Rutherford, Geiger & Marsden

They fired alpha particles at thin gold foil. Most passed straight through (the atom is mostly empty space), but some deflected at large angles and a few bounced back. This disproved the plum pudding model. Rutherford proposed the nuclear model: a small, dense, positively charged nucleus with electrons orbiting around it.

1913

Bohr’s Model

Niels Bohr refined the model by placing electrons in fixed energy levels at specific distances from the nucleus, rather than orbiting randomly.

Key Fact

The alpha scattering experiment disproved the plum pudding model. Most alpha particles passed through (mostly empty space), some bounced back (small, dense, positive nucleus).

Electronic Configuration

Electrons occupy energy levels (shells) around the nucleus. The first shell holds a maximum of 2 electrons. The second and third shells each hold a maximum of 8. Electrons fill the lowest available energy level first.

Find the element’s atomic number (= number of electrons in a neutral atom). Fill the first shell with up to 2, the second with up to 8, and the third with up to 8. For example: oxygen (8 electrons) is 2, 6. Sodium (11 electrons) is 2, 8, 1. Calcium (20 electrons) is 2, 8, 8, 2. The number of outer-shell electrons matches the group number for Groups 1–7, explaining why elements in the same group react similarly.

The electronic configuration determines how an element reacts. Group 1 elements have one outer electron and lose it easily. Group 7 elements have seven outer electrons and tend to gain one. Group 0 elements have full outer shells and are very unreactive.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In calculation questions about subatomic particles, always show your working: number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number. For “describe” questions on the history of the atomic model, name the scientist, state the experiment or evidence, and explain what conclusion was drawn — examiners award separate marks for each step.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Atoms have a small, dense nucleus (protons + neutrons) surrounded by electrons in energy levels. Typical atomic radius is \(1 \times 10^{-10}\) m.
  • Isotopes have the same protons but different neutrons. Ions form when atoms gain or lose electrons — the nucleus does not change.
  • The atomic model evolved through Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr, driven by new experimental evidence at each stage.

lessons.title: Purity and Separating Mixtures
lessons.description: Chemical purity, melting points, filtration, distillation and chromatography.
lessons.content_html:
Pure Substances in Chemistry

In everyday language, “pure” often means natural or uncontaminated. In chemistry, the meaning is very specific: a pure substance is one that contains only a single element or a single compound. For example, pure water contains only \(H_2O\) molecules and nothing else. Orange juice labelled “pure” in a supermarket is not pure in the chemical sense because it is a mixture of water, sugars, citric acid and many other compounds. This distinction between the everyday and scientific meanings of “pure” is frequently tested in the exam.

You can test whether a substance is pure by measuring its melting point. A pure substance has a sharp, precise melting point — it melts at one exact temperature. An impure substance (a mixture) melts over a range of temperatures, and its melting point is lower than expected. Similarly, a pure substance has a fixed boiling point, while an impure substance boils over a range.

Key Fact

In chemistry, a pure substance contains only one element or one compound. A pure substance melts and boils at a single sharp temperature. An impure substance melts over a range of temperatures.

Relative Formula Mass

The relative formula mass (\(M_r\)) of a compound is found by adding up the relative atomic masses (\(A_r\)) of all the atoms in its formula. For example, for water \(H_2O\): \(M_r = (2 \times 1) + 16 = 18\). For calcium carbonate \(CaCO_3\): \(M_r = 40 + 12 + (3 \times 16) = 100\).

You can also deduce the empirical formula of a compound from the relative numbers of atoms present or from a model or diagram. The empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio — for example, glucose \(C_6H_{12}O_6\) has the empirical formula \(CH_2O\) because the ratio of C:H:O is 1:2:1. You may be asked to deduce the empirical formula from a model, a diagram, or data about the relative numbers of atoms present.

Formulations

Many useful materials are formulations — mixtures that have been carefully designed so that each component is present in a measured quantity to give the product specific properties. Examples include alloys (mixtures of metals), paints, medicines, cleaning products and fuels. An alloy such as steel is a formulation of iron with small amounts of carbon and sometimes other metals such as chromium (in stainless steel). Other examples include paints (pigments, binders, solvents in precise ratios), medicines (active ingredient mixed with fillers and flavourings), and even concrete (cement, sand, gravel, water).

Separation Techniques

Because the components of a mixture are not chemically bonded, they can be separated by physical methods. The choice of technique depends on the properties of the substances in the mixture.

Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. The mixture is poured through filter paper in a funnel — the liquid passes through (the filtrate) and the solid stays behind (the residue). Crystallisation separates a dissolved solid (solute) from a solution. The solution is heated gently to evaporate the solvent until crystals begin to form, then left to cool so that more crystals grow. This is used to produce pure, dry samples of salts.

Simple distillation separates a solvent from a solution — for example, water from salt water. The solution is heated until the solvent evaporates, then the vapour is cooled and condensed back into a liquid in a separate container. Fractional distillation separates a mixture of liquids with different boiling points. The mixture is heated in a flask fitted with a fractionating column. The liquid with the lowest boiling point evaporates first, rises to the top of the column, and is collected. Each liquid is collected separately as the temperature rises.

Chromatography

Chromatography separates dissolved substances. It works because different substances have different affinities for a stationary phase (such as paper) and a mobile phase (such as a solvent). In paper chromatography, a spot of the mixture is placed on a pencil line near the bottom of chromatography paper. The paper is placed in a solvent, which rises up the paper carrying the dissolved substances with it. Substances that are more soluble in the mobile phase travel further up the paper.

Key Fact

The \(R_f\) value identifies a substance and is calculated as: $$R_f = \frac{\text{distance moved by substance}}{\text{distance moved by solvent front}}$$ Each substance has a unique \(R_f\) value for a given solvent and stationary phase. A pure substance produces a single spot; a mixture produces multiple spots.

Other chromatographic methods include thin layer chromatography (TLC), which uses a thin layer of silica or alumina on a glass plate as the stationary phase, and gas chromatography, which uses a gas as the mobile phase. Locating agents (such as UV light or ninhydrin spray) may be needed to make colourless spots visible on the chromatogram. Gas chromatography uses a gas as the mobile phase and can separate complex mixtures that would be impossible to analyse by paper chromatography alone.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When describing a separation technique, always state what is being separated and how the technique works. For chromatography questions, show your \(R_f\) calculation clearly, measure both distances from the pencil baseline (not the bottom of the paper), and state whether the substance is pure (one spot) or a mixture (multiple spots).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A chemically pure substance contains only one element or compound and has a sharp melting point. Impure substances melt over a range.
  • Separation techniques include filtration, crystallisation, simple distillation, fractional distillation and chromatography — the choice depends on the properties of the mixture.
  • Chromatography uses a stationary and mobile phase. The \(R_f\) value identifies substances and is calculated as distance moved by substance divided by distance moved by solvent.

lessons.title: Bonding
lessons.description: Ionic, covalent and metallic bonding, electron transfer and sharing, dot-and-cross diagrams.
lessons.content_html:
Why Atoms Bond

Atoms are most stable when they have a full outer shell of electrons. Most atoms do not naturally have a full outer shell, so they bond with other atoms to achieve one. There are three main types of chemical bond: ionic bonding, covalent bonding and metallic bonding. All chemical bonds involve electrostatic forces — the attraction between positive and negative charges. The type of bond that forms depends on whether the atoms involved are metals or non-metals and how many electrons are in their outer shells.

Ionic Bonding

Ionic bonding occurs between metals and non-metals. The metal atom transfers one or more electrons to the non-metal atom. The metal atom loses electrons and becomes a positively charged ion (cation). The non-metal atom gains electrons and becomes a negatively charged ion (anion). The oppositely charged ions are then held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction — this is the ionic bond.

For example, in sodium chloride (NaCl): sodium (2, 8, 1) loses one electron to become \(\text{Na}^+\) (2, 8), and chlorine (2, 8, 7) gains one electron to become \(\text{Cl}^-\) (2, 8, 8). Both ions now have full outer shells, making them stable. In magnesium oxide (MgO), magnesium (2, 8, 2) loses two electrons to become \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\), and oxygen (2, 6) gains two electrons to become \(\text{O}^{2-}\). In an ionic compound, billions of ions are arranged in a regular three-dimensional structure called a giant ionic lattice, where each ion is surrounded by oppositely charged ions in all directions.

Key Fact

In ionic bonding, electrons are transferred from metal to non-metal. The resulting ions have opposite charges and attract each other. Ionic compounds form giant ionic lattices.

Covalent Bonding

Covalent bonding occurs between non-metal atoms. Instead of transferring electrons, the atoms share one or more pairs of electrons. Each shared pair of electrons is one covalent bond. By sharing, both atoms achieve full outer shells. A single shared pair is a single bond, two shared pairs form a double bond (e.g. \(O_2\)), and three shared pairs form a triple bond (e.g. \(N_2\)).

For example, in a molecule of water (\(H_2O\)), the oxygen atom shares one pair of electrons with each of two hydrogen atoms, forming two covalent bonds. In chlorine gas (\(Cl_2\)), two chlorine atoms each share one pair of electrons, forming a single covalent bond. Covalent compounds include small simple molecules (like \(H_2O\), \(CO_2\), \(CH_4\)) and enormous giant covalent structures (like diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide).

Dot-and-cross diagrams show how electrons are arranged in a bond. Use dots for the electrons from one atom and crosses for the electrons from the other. For ionic compounds, show the electron transfer and put each ion in square brackets with its charge. For covalent compounds, show the shared pairs in the overlap between the two atoms. These diagrams are a useful model but have limitations: they do not show the three-dimensional shape of molecules, the relative sizes of atoms, or the distances between atoms. Ball-and-stick models and space-filling models address some of these limitations but introduce others. No single model is perfect — each emphasises different aspects of bonding.

Metallic Bonding

In metals, the atoms are arranged in a regular structure. The outer-shell electrons are delocalised — they are free to move through the whole structure rather than being attached to individual atoms. This leaves behind a lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by a “sea” of delocalised electrons. The strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the negative delocalised electrons is what holds the metal together.

Types of Structure

Substances can have different types of structure, which affects their properties:

Giant ionic lattices (e.g. NaCl) — regular arrangement of alternating positive and negative ions, held by strong ionic bonds in all directions. Simple molecular structures (e.g. \(H_2O\), \(CO_2\)) — small molecules with strong covalent bonds within molecules but weak intermolecular forces between molecules. Giant covalent structures (e.g. diamond, graphite) — huge networks of atoms all bonded by strong covalent bonds. Polymers — very long chain molecules made of repeating units joined by covalent bonds. Metallic structures — regular lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons.

Key Fact

Chemical bonding is always about electrostatic forces: ionic = attraction between opposite ions; covalent = shared electron pairs attracting both nuclei; metallic = positive ions attracted to delocalised electrons.

The Periodic Table helps predict bonding type. Elements on the left (metals) tend to lose electrons. Elements on the right (non-metals) tend to gain or share electrons. An element’s position in the table — its group and period — tells you its electronic configuration, which determines how it bonds. Group 1 elements have one outer electron and form +1 ions; Group 7 elements have seven outer electrons and gain one to form −1 ions. Elements in Group 0 have full outer shells and do not readily bond.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When drawing dot-and-cross diagrams, always show the outer shell electrons clearly. For ionic compounds, use square brackets and include the charge (e.g. [Na]\(^+\)). For covalent compounds, only show the outer shell and make sure each atom achieves a full outer shell through sharing. In “explain” questions about bonding, always refer to electrostatic forces and electron transfer or sharing.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ionic bonding = electron transfer between metals and non-metals, forming a giant ionic lattice of oppositely charged ions.
  • Covalent bonding = electron sharing between non-metals, forming simple molecules or giant covalent structures.
  • Metallic bonding = delocalised electrons shared across a lattice of positive metal ions.

lessons.title: Properties of Materials
lessons.description: How bonding type determines physical properties of ionic, covalent and metallic substances.
lessons.content_html:
Linking Structure to Properties

The physical properties of a substance — its melting point, boiling point, hardness and electrical conductivity — depend on its type of bonding and structure. Understanding this link is one of the most important ideas in chemistry: if you know the bonding, you can predict the properties. The exam frequently tests your ability to explain properties in terms of structure and bonding, so it is essential to link every property back to the forces involved.

Ionic Compounds

Ionic compounds such as sodium chloride have giant ionic lattice structures. They have high melting and boiling points because a large amount of energy is needed to break the many strong electrostatic forces between the ions. They do not conduct electricity when solid because the ions are held in fixed positions. However, they do conduct when molten or dissolved in water because the ions become free to move and carry charge. Ionic compounds are often brittle — when a force is applied, layers of ions shift and like charges line up, causing repulsion that shatters the crystal. Most ionic compounds are also soluble in water because water molecules can surround and separate the individual ions.

Key Fact

Ionic compounds: high melting points (strong ionic bonds), conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved (ions must be free to move), do not conduct as solids (ions fixed in place).

Simple Molecular Substances

Simple molecular substances (such as water, carbon dioxide and oxygen) have strong covalent bonds within each molecule but weak intermolecular forces between molecules. It is these weak intermolecular forces that are overcome when the substance melts or boils — not the covalent bonds. This means simple molecular substances have low melting and boiling points and are often gases or liquids at room temperature. They do not conduct electricity in any state because they have no free electrons or ions to carry charge. It is a very common exam error to say the covalent bonds are weak — the bonds within the molecules are strong; it is the forces between molecules that are weak.

Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces because there are more electrons that can create temporary dipoles. This means larger molecules tend to have higher boiling points. For example, the boiling point of methane (\(CH_4\), small molecule) is much lower than that of octane (\(C_8H_{18}\), larger molecule). The strength of the intermolecular forces depends on the size of the molecule, not the strength of the covalent bonds within it.

Giant Covalent Structures

Giant covalent structures contain billions of atoms all bonded by strong covalent bonds in a continuous network. They have very high melting points because many strong covalent bonds must be broken. Carbon has several giant covalent allotropes — different structural forms of the same element, each with distinct physical properties:

Carbon can form four covalent bonds. In diamond, each carbon atom bonds to four others in a rigid tetrahedral arrangement — making it extremely hard and unable to conduct electricity (no free electrons). In graphite, each carbon bonds to three others in flat hexagonal layers with weak forces between layers, allowing them to slide over each other (making graphite soft and slippery). One electron per carbon atom is delocalised within each layer, so graphite does conduct electricity. Fullerenes (e.g. \(C_{60}\) buckminsterfullerene) are hollow carbon molecules shaped like balls or tubes. Graphene is a single layer of graphite — one atom thick, incredibly strong, an excellent electrical conductor, and a potential material for electronics and composites.

Key Fact

Carbon can form four covalent bonds. Diamond (4 bonds per C, very hard, non-conductor), Graphite (3 bonds per C, layers slide, conducts electricity), Graphene (single layer of graphite, strong, conducts), Fullerenes (hollow molecules, e.g. \(C_{60}\)).

Polymers and Metals

Polymers are very long chain molecules made of repeating units. They are held together by strong covalent bonds along the chain and weaker intermolecular forces between chains. Their properties depend on what the repeating unit is and how the chains are arranged. Metals have high melting points, conduct electricity (delocalised electrons), and are malleable (layers of positive ions can slide over each other without breaking the metallic bond, because the delocalised electrons can adjust to the new positions). Metals are also good conductors of heat because the delocalised electrons transfer kinetic energy quickly through the structure.

You can use data such as melting point and boiling point to predict the state of a substance at a given temperature. If the temperature is below the melting point, the substance is solid. Between melting and boiling point, it is liquid. Above the boiling point, it is a gas. For example, water (melting point 0°C, boiling point 100°C) is solid below 0°C, liquid between 0°C and 100°C, and gas above 100°C. This skill is commonly tested using data tables.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When explaining why a substance has a high or low melting point, always specify what is being broken. For ionic compounds, say “strong electrostatic forces between ions.” For simple molecules, say “weak intermolecular forces between molecules” — never say “weak covalent bonds.” The covalent bonds within the molecules are strong; it’s the forces between molecules that are weak.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ionic compounds have high melting points and conduct when molten/dissolved. Simple molecules have low melting points and do not conduct.
  • Giant covalent structures (diamond, graphite, graphene) have very high melting points. Graphite and graphene conduct electricity due to delocalised electrons.
  • The bulk properties of materials are determined by the type of bonding, the strength of bonds relative to intermolecular forces, and how the bonds are arranged.

lessons.title: Chemical Reactions and Equations
lessons.description: Writing formulae, balancing equations, conservation of mass, and the mole concept.
lessons.content_html:
Chemical Symbols and Formulae

Every element has a unique chemical symbol, shown on the periodic table. Compounds are represented by chemical formulae that show which elements are present and how many atoms of each. For example, \(H_2O\) tells you water contains 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. \(CaCO_3\) tells you calcium carbonate contains 1 calcium, 1 carbon and 3 oxygen atoms. Small subscript numbers apply to the element directly before them; a number before a formula (a coefficient) multiplies every atom in that formula.

Working out the formula of a compound from its name requires knowledge of ion charges. For example, sodium chloride is \(NaCl\) because \(Na^+\) and \(Cl^-\) balance in a 1:1 ratio. Magnesium oxide is \(MgO\) (\(Mg^{2+}\) and \(O^{2-}\)).

Key Fact

Chemical formulae show which elements are present and the ratio of atoms. Subscript numbers apply to the preceding element; coefficients multiply the whole formula. \(H_2O\) = 2 hydrogen + 1 oxygen.

Writing and Balancing Equations

A chemical equation shows reactants on the left and products on the right, separated by an arrow (\(\rightarrow\)). A word equation uses names: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide. A symbol equation uses formulae: \(2Mg + O_2 \rightarrow 2MgO\).

Symbol equations must be balanced so that the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides. This reflects the conservation of mass — atoms are rearranged in reactions but never created or destroyed (C3.1a). To balance an equation: count atoms on each side, add coefficients (large numbers in front of formulae) until both sides match, and never change the subscript numbers in a formula.

Balance the reaction between hydrogen and oxygen to form water:

Unbalanced: \(H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow H_2O\)

Count atoms: Left — 2 H, 2 O. Right — 2 H, 1 O. Oxygen is unbalanced.

Put a 2 in front of \(H_2O\): \(H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O\). Now right side has 4 H and 2 O. Left has 2 H and 2 O. Hydrogen is unbalanced.

Put a 2 in front of \(H_2\): \(2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O\). Now both sides have 4 H and 2 O. Balanced.

Key Fact

Equations must be balanced: same number of atoms on each side. Add coefficients to balance — never change subscript numbers. Conservation of mass: total mass of reactants = total mass of products.

State Symbols

State symbols are written after each formula to show the physical state: (s) = solid, (l) = liquid, (g) = gas, (aq) = aqueous (dissolved in water). For example:

$$2Na(s) + 2H_2O(l) \rightarrow 2NaOH(aq) + H_2(g)$$

State symbols give extra information about reaction conditions and help you understand whether substances are dissolved, gaseous, etc.

Conservation of mass can be demonstrated experimentally. If you carry out a reaction in a sealed container and measure the total mass before and after, it remains the same. In open containers, reactions that produce gas may appear to lose mass (because the gas escapes), but the total mass of all products — including the gas — equals the total mass of reactants.

An important application of balanced equations is calculating reacting masses. Using relative atomic masses from the periodic table, you can work out how much product will form from a given amount of reactant. For example, from \(2Mg + O_2 \rightarrow 2MgO\): 2 moles of magnesium (48 g) react with 1 mole of oxygen (32 g) to form 2 moles of magnesium oxide (80 g). This confirms conservation of mass: 48 + 32 = 80.

You should also be aware of the difference between exothermic reactions (which release energy to the surroundings, causing a temperature rise, e.g. combustion and neutralisation) and endothermic reactions (which absorb energy from the surroundings, causing a temperature drop, e.g. thermal decomposition and dissolving ammonium nitrate in water). Energy changes during reactions are linked to the breaking and forming of chemical bonds.

Breaking bonds requires energy (endothermic process), while forming bonds releases energy (exothermic process). In an exothermic reaction, the energy released by forming new bonds exceeds the energy needed to break existing bonds, so the overall reaction releases energy to the surroundings and the temperature rises. In an endothermic reaction, the opposite is true — more energy is needed to break bonds than is released when new bonds form.

Types of Chemical Reaction

OCR Gateway requires knowledge of several reaction types (C3.1b):

• Combustion: a substance reacts with oxygen, releasing energy. \(CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O\)
• Displacement: a more reactive element replaces a less reactive one. \(Zn + CuSO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + Cu\)
• Neutralisation: acid + base → salt + water. \(HCl + NaOH \rightarrow NaCl + H_2O\)
• Oxidation: gaining oxygen (or losing electrons). Reduction: losing oxygen (or gaining electrons). Redox reactions involve both.
• Thermal decomposition: a substance breaks down when heated. \(CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2\)

Key Fact

Key reaction types: combustion (fuel + oxygen), displacement (reactive metal replaces less reactive one), neutralisation (acid + base → salt + water), thermal decomposition (breaks down with heat). All must be balanced.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For OCR Gateway equation questions, always check your equation is balanced by counting every atom on both sides. Include state symbols if asked. When given a word equation and asked for a symbol equation, write the formulae first, then balance. A common mistake is changing the subscript numbers instead of adding coefficients — this changes the compound itself.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Chemical formulae show element types and atom ratios. Equations must be balanced to reflect conservation of mass.
  • Balance equations by adding coefficients (not by changing subscripts). State symbols (s), (l), (g), (aq) show physical states.
  • Know the key reaction types: combustion, displacement, neutralisation, oxidation/reduction and thermal decomposition.

lessons.title: Energetics
lessons.description: Exothermic and endothermic reactions, reaction profiles, activation energy and bond energies.
lessons.content_html:
Energy Changes in Reactions

Every chemical reaction involves an energy change. Energy is either transferred to the surroundings or absorbed from them. The key principle is that energy is transferred, never created or destroyed. Two categories describe the direction of energy transfer. Understanding these categories — and the bond-level explanation for why energy is transferred — is fundamental to the whole of chemistry. Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between the system and the surroundings.

Key Fact

Exothermic reactions transfer energy to the surroundings — the temperature of the surroundings increases. Endothermic reactions take in energy from the surroundings — the temperature of the surroundings decreases.

Exothermic reactions include combustion (burning fuels), neutralisation (acid + alkali), and many oxidation reactions. Everyday examples include hand warmers (the crystallisation of a supersaturated sodium acetate solution) and self-heating food cans. Endothermic reactions include thermal decomposition, the reaction of citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate, thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate, and photosynthesis. Sports cold packs are a practical example — the endothermic dissolution of ammonium nitrate in water absorbs heat, cooling the injured area.

Measuring Energy Changes (PAG C5)

You can identify whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic by measuring the temperature change of the surroundings (usually a solution in a polystyrene cup). If the temperature rises, the reaction is exothermic. If the temperature falls, the reaction is endothermic. A polystyrene cup is used as an insulator to reduce heat loss to the surroundings, giving a more accurate temperature reading. You should record the starting temperature, the maximum (or minimum) temperature, and calculate the change. In a well-insulated system, a bigger temperature change indicates a more energetic reaction.

Reaction Profiles

A reaction profile is a diagram that shows the energy levels of the reactants and products, and the energy change during a reaction. On the vertical axis is energy; on the horizontal axis is the progress of the reaction (sometimes labelled “reaction pathway”). The diagram does not show time — it simply shows the energy changes as reactants transform into products.

For an exothermic reaction, the products are at a lower energy level than the reactants — the energy difference has been released to the surroundings. The profile shows a “hump” from reactants rising to a peak (the activation energy barrier) then falling to a lower product level. For an endothermic reaction, the products are at a higher energy level than the reactants — energy has been absorbed. The profile shows a hump rising to the peak then settling at a level higher than the starting point. In both cases, the hump represents the activation energy — the minimum energy needed for the reaction to start. You must label four things on any reaction profile: the energy level of reactants, the energy level of products, the activation energy (from reactants to the peak), and the overall energy change (from reactants to products).

Key Fact

Activation energy is the minimum energy that colliding particles need for a reaction to occur. It is shown on a reaction profile as the difference between the reactant energy level and the top of the energy barrier (the peak).

Bond Energy Calculations (Higher)

During a chemical reaction, bonds in the reactants must be broken (this requires energy — endothermic) and new bonds in the products are made (this releases energy — exothermic). The overall energy change depends on the balance between these two processes. This is a Higher Tier calculation that requires you to use given bond energy values:

Step 1: Add up the total energy needed to break all the bonds in the reactants. Step 2: Add up the total energy released when all the bonds in the products are formed. Step 3: Calculate the overall energy change:

$$\text{energy change} = \text{energy to break bonds} - \text{energy released making bonds}$$

If the answer is positive, the reaction is endothermic (more energy needed to break bonds than is released making them). If the answer is negative, the reaction is exothermic (more energy released making bonds than needed to break them).

For example, for \(H_2 + Cl_2 \rightarrow 2HCl\): breaking bonds = H–H (436 kJ) + Cl–Cl (242 kJ) = 678 kJ. Making bonds = 2 × H–Cl (431 kJ) = 862 kJ. Energy change = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ. Negative, so exothermic. More energy was released making the H–Cl bonds than was required to break the H–H and Cl–Cl bonds, so the surplus energy is transferred to the surroundings as heat. This is why the overall reaction is exothermic. Remember: you must always consider all bonds broken and all bonds made, not just some of them.

Key Fact

Breaking bonds requires energy (endothermic). Making bonds releases energy (exothermic). If more energy is released making bonds than absorbed breaking them, the reaction is exothermic overall.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For reaction profile questions, always label the axes (energy on the y-axis, progress of reaction on the x-axis) and draw clear arrows showing the activation energy and the overall energy change. For bond energy calculations, set out your working clearly in two columns: “bonds broken” and “bonds made.” Show the subtraction step. A negative answer = exothermic; positive = endothermic.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Exothermic reactions release energy (temperature rises); endothermic reactions absorb energy (temperature falls).
  • Reaction profiles show energy levels of reactants and products, the activation energy barrier, and whether the overall change is exothermic or endothermic.
  • Bond energy calculations: overall energy change = energy to break bonds − energy released making bonds. Negative = exothermic, positive = endothermic.

• The overall energy change = energy to break bonds – energy released making bonds.

lessons.title: Types of Chemical Reactions and Electrolysis
lessons.description: Redox, acids, neutralisation, pH scale, and electrolysis of molten and aqueous compounds.
lessons.content_html:
Oxidation and Reduction

Oxidation is the gain of oxygen or the loss of electrons. Reduction is the loss of oxygen or the gain of electrons. These always happen together in what are called redox reactions. A useful mnemonic is OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

For example, when copper oxide is reduced by carbon: \(2CuO + C \rightarrow 2Cu + CO_2\). The copper oxide loses oxygen (it is reduced) and the carbon gains oxygen (it is oxidised). Carbon is the reducing agent (it causes the reduction of copper oxide) and copper oxide is the oxidising agent (it causes the oxidation of carbon). At Higher Tier, you also need to explain redox in terms of electrons: the substance that is oxidised loses electrons, and the substance that is reduced gains electrons. For example, in the formation of magnesium oxide: \(Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + 2e^-\) (oxidation) and \(O + 2e^- \rightarrow O^{2-}\) (reduction).

Key Fact

Oxidation = gain of oxygen OR loss of electrons. Reduction = loss of oxygen OR gain of electrons. In terms of electrons (Higher): the substance that is oxidised loses electrons; the substance that is reduced gains electrons.

Acids and Alkalis

Acids produce hydrogen ions (\(H^+\)) when they dissolve in water. Solutions of alkalis contain hydroxide ions (\(OH^-\)). The pH scale measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is, running from 0 (very strong acid) to 14 (very strong alkali). pH 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic, and above 7 is alkaline. Each step on the pH scale represents a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration.

You can measure pH using universal indicator (which changes colour across a range: red for strong acids, green for neutral, purple for strong alkalis) or a pH meter (which gives a precise numerical reading). Litmus paper gives a simple acid/alkali test but cannot distinguish between different strengths.

Dilute and concentrated refer to the amount of acid dissolved in a given volume of water. Strong and weak refer to the degree of ionisation. A strong acid (e.g. hydrochloric acid) fully ionises in water — every molecule produces \(H^+\) ions. A weak acid (e.g. ethanoic acid) only partially ionises — only some molecules produce \(H^+\) ions. When the hydrogen ion concentration increases by a factor of ten, the pH decreases by one.

Neutralisation and Making Salts

Neutralisation occurs when an acid reacts with a base or alkali to form a salt plus water. The ionic equation for neutralisation is:

$$H^+(aq) + OH^-(aq) \rightarrow H_2O(l)$$

Key reactions to know:

Acid + metal \(\rightarrow\) salt + hydrogen. For example: \(Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) \rightarrow MgCl_2(aq) + H_2(g)\).

Acid + metal carbonate \(\rightarrow\) salt + water + carbon dioxide. For example: \(CaCO_3(s) + 2HCl(aq) \rightarrow CaCl_2(aq) + H_2O(l) + CO_2(g)\).

Acid + alkali \(\rightarrow\) salt + water. For example: \(NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) \rightarrow NaCl(aq) + H_2O(l)\).

Key Fact

The name of the salt depends on the acid used: hydrochloric acid \(\rightarrow\) chloride salts, sulfuric acid \(\rightarrow\) sulfate salts, nitric acid \(\rightarrow\) nitrate salts.

Electrolysis

Electrolysis is the process of using an electric current to decompose (break down) an ionic compound that is either molten or dissolved in water. The ionic compound must be in a liquid state (molten or dissolved in water) so that the ions are free to move and carry the electrical current. Solid ionic compounds cannot be electrolysed because their ions are held in fixed positions within the lattice.

The ionic compound is placed in a container with two electrodes connected to a power supply. Positive ions (cations) move towards the cathode (negative electrode), where they gain electrons and are reduced. Negative ions (anions) move towards the anode (positive electrode), where they lose electrons and are oxidised. Metals (or hydrogen) form at the cathode; non-metals form at the anode.

For molten binary compounds, predicting products is straightforward. For example, molten sodium chloride produces sodium at the cathode and chlorine at the anode. For aqueous solutions, there are competing reactions because water also contains \(H^+\) and \(OH^-\) ions. At the cathode, hydrogen is produced instead of the metal if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen. At the anode, oxygen is usually produced (from \(OH^-\) ions) unless halide ions are present, in which case the halogen is produced. For example, electrolysing aqueous copper sulfate with inert (carbon) electrodes produces copper at the cathode (because copper is less reactive than hydrogen) and oxygen at the anode (because no halide ions are present). The electrodes used matter: inert electrodes (such as carbon or platinum) do not take part in the reaction, whereas non-inert electrodes (such as copper) can themselves dissolve or be deposited during electrolysis.

Key Fact

At the cathode: \(\text{Na}^+ + e^- \rightarrow \text{Na}\) (reduction). At the anode: \(2\text{Cl}^- \rightarrow Cl_2 + 2e^-\) (oxidation). Half equations show what happens at each electrode separately.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For electrolysis questions, always identify whether the compound is molten or aqueous — this changes the products. Write half equations for each electrode and state whether oxidation or reduction occurs. For acid reactions, be systematic: identify the acid, the base/metal/carbonate, and then predict the salt name. Show balanced equations with state symbols where possible.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of electrons (OIL RIG). Reduction is the reverse. These always occur together in redox reactions.
  • Acids produce \(H^+\) ions; alkalis produce \(OH^-\) ions. Neutralisation: \(H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O\). Salt names depend on the acid used.
  • Electrolysis decomposes ionic compounds using electricity. Cations go to the cathode (reduced); anions go to the anode (oxidised).

practice_questions.text: Aqueous copper sulfate solution is electrolysed using inert (carbon) electrodes. Discuss what products form at each electrode and explain why these products form rather than alternatives. Include half equations in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:

Mid band (3-4): Identifies products with some explanation or partial half equations.
Lower band (1-2): Names one or both products with limited explanation.
Indicative content:
• Cathode: copper is deposited (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu) because copper is less reactive than hydrogen.
• Anode: oxygen gas is produced (4OH⁻ → 2H₂O + O₂ + 4e⁻) because sulfate ions are not discharged / OH⁻ ions from water are discharged preferentially (no halide ions present).
• The solution contains Cu²⁺, SO₄²⁻, H⁺ and OH⁻ ions.
• At the cathode, Cu²⁺ is preferentially discharged because Cu is less reactive than H.
• At the anode, OH⁻ is preferentially discharged because no halide ions are present.
